title: Locks on hearts
hook: do they not reflect on the Qur'an, or are there locks on their hearts (47:24)

segments.voice: Yesterday, help Him, and He helps you, and your line was feet made firm. Did you plant your feet for something right? Day five hundred seventy-nine.

You can read a page and arrive at the bottom with no idea what was on it. Eyes moved. Mind was elsewhere. Everyone has done it with a contract, a textbook, an email from their boss. People do it with scripture too, sometimes beautifully: a flawless recitation, every vowel in place, and nothing reaching the heart. Surah Muhammad has a question about that. And it uses a picture you can almost hear: a lock, clicking shut.

Verse twenty-four, in Pickthall's translation: "Will they then not meditate on the Qur'an, or are there locks on the hearts?" The Arabic verb behind meditate is yatadabbarun, and its noun is tadabbur. The root d-b-r means the back of something, what comes after. Lexicons explain tadabbur as looking at the end of a matter, thinking through where a thing leads. So tadabbur isn't just reading. It's following a verse past its last word: what does this ask of me, where does it take me, what changes if I mean it. The Qur'an asks for this more than once. Surah An-Nisa' asks the same question, will they not ponder the Qur'an. Surah Sad says the book was sent down, blessed, so that people would ponder its verses and those with understanding would take heed. Then the lock. The verse says locks, plural, on hearts, plural, and the Arabic adds a small word, aqfaluha, their locks, as if each heart has a lock fitted to it. Commentators read it as a heart sealed by habit, pride or carelessness until nothing can get in. The question isn't an accusation thrown at outsiders. Many scholars treat it as a mirror for believers, especially the ones who read often. The early generations were known for reading slowly. Reports describe Companions who would spend a whole night on a single verse, repeating it. The point wasn't how far they got. It was how deep.
screen: `TADABBUR: FOLLOW A VERSE PAST ITS END.` · `D-B-R: THE BACK, WHAT COMES AFTER.` · `EACH HEART WITH ITS OWN LOCK.` · `ONE VERSE, ALL NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The outline asks for five minutes on one verse; start with the two the bell gives you. Take today's verse: will they not meditate, or are there locks on the hearts. Say it slowly in your head. Then ask the three questions of tadabbur. What does it say? What does it ask of me? Where does it lead, if I mean it? Stay with whichever question opens something. If you pray, you can ask for the lock to open. The bell holds the time.
Tadabbur. Pondering that follows a verse past its last word, from the root for what comes after, asked for in 47:24. Today's word.
Your line: unlock the heart. Today, read one thing slowly, a verse, a letter, a message from someone you love, and follow it one step past the last word. Day five hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Alongside recitation, many Muslims join tadabbur circles or read a few verses daily with a tafsir, pausing to ask what each verse asks of them; some repeat a single verse many times in night prayer.
